clock.docs: Current UTC timestamp as ISO-8601 string.
clock.name: now

clock.docs: Format an RFC3339 timestamp with a strftime pattern, e.g. `%Y-%m-%d`. Answers `ok(string)`, or `err` if the timestamp or the pattern is not valid.
clock.name: format

clock.docs: Sleep for a duration in milliseconds.
clock.name: sleep

clock.docs: Shift an RFC3339 timestamp by a duration, which takes the same forms as `@clock.duration` — an integer of milliseconds or a string like `7d`, `-1h`, `30m`. Answers `ok(timestamp)` or `err`.
clock.name: add

clock.docs: Milliseconds from `b` to `a`, i.e. `a - b`. Positive when `a` is later. Answers `ok(int)` or `err` if either is not RFC3339.
clock.name: diff

clock.docs: Normalize a duration to whole milliseconds. Accepts an integer or float of milliseconds, or a string with a unit: `250ms`, `2s`, `5m`, `1h`, `1d`. Answers `ok(int)` or `err`.
clock.name: duration

console.docs: Write a value to stdout without a trailing newline.
console.name: print

console.docs: Write a value to stdout with a trailing newline.
console.name: println

console.docs: Write a debug representation to stdout.
console.name: inspect

console.docs: Read one line from stdin, after writing the optional prompt without a trailing newline. The line comes back without its terminator (`\n` or `\r\n`); end of input answers the empty string. The prompt is written by the runtime, which owns the output sink, so this is called with no argument from there.
console.name: read_line

crypto.docs: SHA-256 digest of a string, as lowercase hex.
crypto.name: sha256

crypto.docs: SHA-512 digest of a string, as lowercase hex.
crypto.name: sha512

crypto.docs: HMAC-SHA-256 of a message under a key, as lowercase hex.
crypto.name: hmac_sha256

crypto.docs: n cryptographically secure random bytes, as lowercase hex.
crypto.name: random_bytes

crypto.docs: Compare two strings in time independent of their contents.
crypto.name: constant_time_eq

crypto.docs: Encode a string as standard base64 (RFC 4648, padded).
crypto.name: base64_encode

crypto.docs: Decode standard base64 to a string. Answers a Result.
crypto.name: base64_decode

crypto.docs: Encode a string as lowercase hex.
crypto.name: hex_encode

crypto.docs: Decode hex to a string. Answers a Result.
crypto.name: hex_decode

csv.docs: Parse a CSV string into a list of records (ok/err). Options: headers (default true), delimiter, skip_empty.
csv.name: decode

csv.docs: Serialize a list of records (or list of lists) to a CSV string.
csv.name: encode

csv.docs: Read and parse a CSV file into a list of records.
csv.name: read

csv.docs: Write a list of records as CSV to a file.
csv.name: write

db.docs: Open a DuckDB connection. Path omitted or ":memory:" → in-memory. Needs --allow db or --allow db=path. DuckDB's own file/network access (read_csv, COPY TO, ATTACH, extensions) is sandboxed to the granted db= / fs:write roots.
db.name: open

db.docs: Execute SQL that does not return rows (DDL/DML). Optional params list.
db.name: exec

db.docs: Run a SQL query and return ok(list of records). Optional params list.
db.name: query

db.docs: Prepare a SQL statement; returns a statement handle.
db.name: prepare

db.docs: Execute a prepared statement as a query. Optional params list.
db.name: query_prepared

db.docs: Execute a prepared statement without returning rows. Optional params list.
db.name: exec_prepared

db.docs: BEGIN a transaction on the connection.
db.name: begin

env.docs: Get an environment variable or none.
env.name: get

env.docs: Get a required environment variable as result.
env.name: require

env.docs: Return the environment variables this script may read, as a record. With `--allow env` that is everything; with `--allow env=NAME,…` it is exactly the names granted. Denied when nothing is granted.
env.name: all

env.docs: Set an environment variable for this run. Needs `--allow env:write` (or `env:write=NAME`), which is a *separate* grant from the `env` read permission. The value is visible to `@env.get`, `@env.require` and `@env.all`, and is inherited by commands started with `@process.run`. It does not modify the operating-system environment of this process: writing that is unsafe while other threads are running, and a program started outside `@process.run` will not see it.
env.name: set

fs.docs: Read file lines as a list of strings.
fs.name: lines

fs.docs: Open a file and answer a handle: `! @fs.open(path, #read)?`. Modes are `#read`, `#write` (creates, truncates) and `#append` (creates, keeps). The permission is decided here — `#read` needs `fs:read` for the path, the other two need `fs:write` — so the reads and writes that follow need no further grant. A handle is closed with `@fs.close`, or when the run ends; one run may hold 1024 open at once.
fs.name: open

fs.docs: Read up to `n` bytes from an open handle, answering `ok(bytes)`. Fewer than `n` means the end of the file is near; **empty** means it has been reached. Unlike `@fs.read_bytes`, peak memory is the chunk rather than the file.
fs.name: read_chunk

fs.docs: Read one line from an open handle, without its line ending. Answers `ok(none)` at the end of the file — an empty line is `ok("")`, which is a different thing, and why this reports the end with `none` rather than an empty string.
fs.name: read_line

fs.docs: Write text or bytes to a handle opened `#write` or `#append`, answering `ok(count)` of bytes written. Buffered: call `@fs.flush` or `@fs.close` to be sure it reached the disk.
fs.name: write_chunk

fs.docs: Move an open handle to a byte offset from the start of the file, answering `ok(position)`. A negative offset counts back from the end, as `slice` does.
fs.name: seek

fs.docs: Push a write handle's buffered bytes to the file. `@fs.close` flushes too; this is for when you want the bytes there and the handle still open.
fs.name: flush

fs.docs: Close an open handle, flushing it first. Closing one that is already closed is `ok`, not an error — a script that closes on both the success and the failure path is being careful, not wrong.
fs.name: close

fs.docs: Return a file metadata record: `len`, `is_file`, `is_dir`, `is_symlink`, and `mtime` as an RFC3339 UTC string (comparable against `@clock.now`). Follows symlinks, so every field but `is_symlink` describes the target.
fs.name: metadata

fs.docs: Expand a glob pattern to matching paths. The pattern must point inside a granted read root; matches outside every granted root are dropped.
fs.name: glob

fs.docs: Remove a file, or a directory and everything inside it. Recursive and irreversible, like `rm -rf`.
fs.name: remove

game.docs: Serialize game state to JSON string.
game.name: save

game.docs: Load game state from JSON string.
game.name: load

game.docs: Parse and run a player command.
game.name: command

http.docs: Start an HTTP server and block until shutdown. Loopback (127.0.0.0/8, ::1, localhost) binds by default; any other interface — including the wildcards 0.0.0.0 and [::] — needs --allow net=<host>.
http.name: listen

http.docs: GET a URL. Returns ok(response) or err(record). Needs --allow net=<host>.
http.name: get

http.docs: POST a body to a URL. A record body is sent as JSON, a string as-is. Needs --allow net=<host>.
http.name: post

http.docs: Send a request described by a record: <<method, url, headers, body, timeout_ms>>. Needs --allow net=<host>.
http.name: request

http.docs: Build an explicit response record `⟨status, body, headers⟩`. Body and headers are optional; the body defaults to `none` and an explicit `content-type` header overrides the one inferred from the body.
http.name: response

http.docs: Read a file under `root` and build a response for it, with `content-type` from the extension. The subpath cannot escape `root`. A directory resolves to its `index.html`. Returns ok(response) or err(record). Needs `--allow fs:read=<root>`.
http.name: file

http.docs: Middleware: log each request as `rite: METHOD path status duration` to stderr. Enable with `use @http.log` or `⊏ @http.log`.
http.name: log

http.docs: Middleware: convert handler panics/errors into JSON 500 responses. Enable with `use @http.recover` or `⊏ @http.recover`.
http.name: recover

json.docs: Parse a JSON string into a Rite value.
json.name: decode

json.docs: Serialize a value to compact JSON.
json.name: encode

json.docs: Serialize a value to pretty JSON.
json.name: encode_pretty

json.docs: Read and parse a JSON file.
json.name: read

json.docs: Write a value as JSON to a file.
json.name: write

mcp.docs: Serve the Model Context Protocol and block until shutdown. Takes a server name, or a config record `⟨name, version, transport, addr, instructions⟩` where `transport` is `#stdio` (the default) or `#http`. Each `tool`, `resource` and `prompt` in the block is published to the client, with its JSON Schema derived from the parameter types declared on it. Under `#http` the bind address needs `--allow net=<host>` unless it is loopback; `#stdio` needs no grant, being the process's own streams.
mcp.name: serve

mcp.docs: Report progress from inside a tool body: `! @mcp.progress(0.5, "halfway")`. Sends a `notifications/progress` on the stream of the call being served. Only valid inside an `@mcp.serve` body — elsewhere it fails rather than silently doing nothing.
mcp.name: progress

mcp.docs: Middleware marker: `use @mcp.log` inside an `@mcp.serve` block writes one structured JSON line per request to stderr. Stderr rather than the protocol's own logging notifications, which are deprecated, and because under `#stdio` stdout carries the wire.
mcp.name: log

mcp.docs: The JSON Schema a function would be published with, derived from its declared parameter types: `@mcp.tool_schema(add)`. Pure — for checking what a tool advertises without starting a server.
mcp.name: tool_schema

mcp.docs: Open a connection to another MCP server and return `ok(handle)`. The spec is a record naming one transport: `⟨command: "npx", args: ["-y", "…"]⟩` starts a server as a subprocess and speaks JSON-RPC on its stdin and stdout, and `⟨url: "https://example.com/mcp"⟩` posts to a Streamable HTTP endpoint. Also understands `env` (record, stdio only), `headers` (record, HTTP only) and `timeout_ms` (default 30000, the ceiling on every request made through the handle). **A `command` spec needs `--allow process`; a `url` spec needs `--allow net=<host>`** — the grant is checked here and nowhere else, so the calls that take the handle need none of their own.
mcp.name: connect

mcp.docs: What a connected server offers: `ok([⟨name, description, input_schema⟩])`. `input_schema` is the tool's JSON Schema, as a record.
mcp.name: tools

mcp.docs: Call a tool on a connected server: `! @mcp.call_tool(c, "add", ⟨a: 2, b: 3⟩)`. Answers `ok(value)` — the structured result if the server sent one, otherwise the text of its content blocks. A tool that fails in band (`isError`) is `err(⟨kind: "mcp.tool_error", tool, message, data⟩)` rather than a raise, so the reason is readable and the call can be retried. `message` is the failure's text; `data` is its own fields, present only when the server sent a structured failure.
mcp.name: call_tool

mcp.docs: What a connected server publishes: `ok([⟨uri, name, description⟩])`.
mcp.name: resources

mcp.docs: Read one resource by URI: `! @mcp.read_resource(c, "config://app")`. Answers `ok(text)`, the contents joined with newlines; a JSON resource comes back as its text, which `@json.decode` parses.
mcp.name: read_resource

mcp.docs: What prompts a connected server offers: `ok([⟨name, description, arguments⟩])`, where each argument is `⟨name, required⟩`.
mcp.name: prompts

mcp.docs: Render a prompt: `! @mcp.get_prompt(c, "review", ⟨code: src⟩)`. Answers `ok(⟨description, messages⟩)`, with each message `⟨role, text⟩`.
mcp.name: get_prompt

mcp.docs: Close a connection handle. Under stdio the server is sent EOF and then stopped. Closing an unknown or already-closed handle answers ok(none), and every connection closes when the run ends.
mcp.name: close

process.docs: Run a command with an argument list (no shell). Answers `ok(⟨status, stdout, stderr⟩)`; a non-zero exit is still `ok`, but a command that cannot be started raises. The third argument is an options record understanding `cwd` (string) and `env` (record, added to the inherited environment); any other key is an error.
process.name: run

process.docs: Arguments passed to this script after `--`, as a list of strings. Needs no permission: they are the invoker's own input to this program, not ambient state.
process.name: args

process.docs: End the run immediately with a chosen exit status, 0–255. Nothing after the call runs, and the status cannot be caught or overridden. Buffered output is still flushed. Needs no permission: choosing your own exit status is the invoker's own business, like reading `@process.args`. Note that 1–8 are also the statuses the runtime itself uses (1 runtime error, 5 permission denied, 8 budget); a script that picks one takes over that meaning for its own process.
process.name: exit

process.docs: Locate an executable on PATH. Reads the PATH environment variable and probes the filesystem, so it is effectful (`!`) and needs process *and* env access to PATH (--allow process --allow env=PATH).
process.name: which

proto.docs: Compile `.proto` source text into a schema handle. Answers `ok(handle)`, or `err` naming the line that failed to parse.
proto.name: compile

proto.docs: Compile several `.proto` sources that import each other, as a record of file name to source. Answers `ok(handle)`.
proto.name: compile_all

proto.docs: Read and compile a `.proto` file, resolving its imports from the containing directory. Answers `ok(handle)`.
proto.name: load_file

proto.docs: Build a schema handle from an encoded `FileDescriptorSet` (`protoc --descriptor_set_out`). Answers `ok(handle)`.
proto.name: load_set

proto.docs: Decode bytes as the named message. Answers `ok(record)` holding only the fields the message actually set.
proto.name: decode

proto.docs: Encode a record as the named message. Answers `ok(bytes)`, or `err` for a key that is not a field of that message.
proto.name: encode

proto.docs: Every message type the schema defines, as a list of fully-qualified names.
proto.name: messages

random.docs: Choose a random element from a list.
random.name: choose

random.docs: Return a shuffled copy of a list.
random.name: shuffle

random.docs: Reseed the RNG for deterministic sequences.
random.name: seed

regex.docs: Whether the pattern matches anywhere in the text. Answers `ok(bool)`, or `err` for a pattern that does not compile.
regex.name: is_match

regex.docs: The first match of the pattern in the text, as `ok(string)` — `ok(none)` when nothing matches.
regex.name: find

regex.docs: Every non-overlapping match, in order, as `ok(list)`.
regex.name: find_all

regex.docs: The first match's groups as `ok(list)` — the whole match first, then each group, `none` for a group that did not participate. `ok(none)` when nothing matches.
regex.name: captures

regex.docs: Every match replaced. `$1`, `$2`, `${name}` in the replacement refer to capture groups. Answers `ok(string)`.
regex.name: replace

regex.docs: The text split around every match of the pattern, as `ok(list)`.
regex.name: split

stdin.docs: The whole of standard input as one string, read to EOF on first use and cached. Empty when nothing was piped in.
stdin.name: read

stdin.docs: Standard input as a list of lines, without their terminators. An empty input is an empty list, so a pipeline over `@stdin.lines` runs zero times rather than once over `""`.
stdin.name: lines

store.docs: Get a value from an in-memory namespace.
store.name: get

store.docs: Set a value in an in-memory namespace.
store.name: set

store.docs: Delete a key from a namespace.
store.name: delete

sys.docs: The process's current working directory, as a string. Effectful: it is where relative paths resolve from, and it is not a constant. Native only.
sys.name: cwd

sys.docs: The invoking user's home directory, or `none` when the platform does not say. Read from `HOME` (or `USERPROFILE` on Windows) but gated on `sys` rather than `env`, because it is asking where the user lives rather than reading their environment. Native only.
sys.name: home

sys.docs: The directory the platform offers for temporary files, as a string. Nothing is created; writing there still needs an `fs:write` grant. Native only.
sys.name: temp_dir

sys.docs: The operating system this is running on: `linux`, `macos`, `windows`, `wasm`, and so on. `std::env::consts::OS`.
sys.name: os

sys.docs: The processor architecture: `x86_64`, `aarch64`, `wasm32`, and so on. `std::env::consts::ARCH`.
sys.name: arch

sys.docs: This process's identifier, as an integer. Native only.
sys.name: pid

sys.docs: The machine's hostname, or `none` when it cannot be determined. Native only.
sys.name: hostname

tcp.docs: Open a TCP connection to "host:port" and return ok(handle). Needs --allow net=<host> for the destination, including loopback. Gives up after 30 seconds with err(⟨kind: "tcp.timeout", …⟩).
tcp.name: connect

tcp.docs: Write the whole payload to a connection. The payload is a string (sent as UTF-8) or a bytes value (sent verbatim). Returns ok(bytes sent).
tcp.name: send

tcp.docs: Read up to max_bytes (default 65536), waiting at most timeout_ms (default 1000). Returns ok(bytes) — **empty** when the peer closed the stream cleanly — or err(⟨kind: "tcp.timeout", …⟩) when nothing arrived in time. Neither is a raise.
tcp.name: recv

tcp.docs: The address at the other end of a connection, as "host:port". Returns ok(string). In a @tcp.listen block this is the client that connected — what a server logs.
tcp.name: peer_addr

tcp.docs: This end of a connection, as "host:port". Returns ok(string). Useful on a client, where the source port is assigned rather than chosen.
tcp.name: local_addr

tcp.docs: Close a connection handle. Closing an unknown or already-closed handle answers ok(none).
tcp.name: close

tcp.docs: Accept TCP connections and run a block per connection: `! @tcp.listen "127.0.0.1:9000" ⟦ |conn| … ⟧`. Blocks until shutdown (Ctrl-C), like @http.listen; the connection is closed when the block returns. Loopback binds by default; any other interface — including the wildcards 0.0.0.0 and [::] — needs --allow net=<host>.
tcp.name: listen

udp.docs: Bind a UDP socket and return ok(handle). Loopback (127.0.0.0/8, ::1, localhost) binds by default; any other interface — including the wildcards 0.0.0.0 and [::] — needs --allow net=<host>. Port 0 picks a free port; read it back with @udp.local_addr.
udp.name: bind

udp.docs: The address a socket is actually bound to, as "host:port". Returns ok(string).
udp.name: local_addr

udp.docs: Send one datagram to "host:port". The payload is a string (sent as UTF-8) or a bytes value (sent verbatim). Returns ok(bytes sent). Needs --allow net=<host> for the destination.
udp.name: send_to

udp.docs: Wait up to timeout_ms (default 1000) for one datagram. Returns ok(⟨from, data, text⟩) — `data` is bytes, `text` is the same payload as lossy UTF-8 — or err(⟨kind: "udp.timeout", …⟩) when nothing arrives. A timeout is a value, not a raise.
udp.name: recv_from

udp.docs: Close a socket handle. Closing an unknown or already-closed handle answers ok(none).
udp.name: close
